I'm currently re-reading Clarke's "The Fountains of Paradise", and it's interesting how dated the style is. Clarke is really a writer whose style was formed in the 1930s and 1940s, and he never really advanced from that. What I find most interesting about his books, in retrospect, is his immensely slow, painful coming out, which his books on re-reading pre-figure. Plotwise I find his books interesting, but, as another has remarked, the major problem with Clarke is that his plots move very slowly. He takes the best part of 12 chapters in "The Fountains of Paradise" to get to the first main plot point, and because he tends to be more interested in physics and engineering his ability to cope with character development is poor. That said, when he writes well his writing really grips you. My favorites/the ones I recommend are "A Fall of Moondust", "The Sands of Mars" and "Islands in the Sky". "The City and the Stars" and "Childhood's End" stand up less well, but are still worth a read. "Rendez-vous with Rama" is a bit slow by modern standards, but as a study of a potential alien artifact it stands up very well.

I've never been as huge a fan of Asimov as other people seem to be. I've read most of his fiction and quite a lot of his non-fiction too, and on balance I prefer him as an explicator of science, rather than a writer of fiction. He was a pretty good short story writer at the time, but much of his short story work has not stood up well. That said, there's so much of it that it's more or less statistically inevitable that some of it is very good. "The Singing Bell" is a very clever SF mystery, and "Nightfall" is justifiably regarded as a classic. Like Clarke, Asimov is hopeless at characterisation, and I've never yet felt any personal involvement with any of his characters: I find they move like shadow puppets, continually presenting the same silhouette. Where Asimov does reasonably well is in his robotics stories, and in the original three of the "Foundation" trilogy. These work because the plots are clever. In the robotics stories Asimov gives himself just enough constraints to present interesting "problem stories", long a staple of the SF genre. Similarly, "Foundation" and its two successors provide clever plotting and interesting solutions to social puzzles. I agree with another poster that "The Mule" is Asimov's most interesting character, but this is perhaps because he is seen more through his actions than as a visible character. Interestingly, the "Foundation" series also contains Asimov's only memorable female character in Arcadia ("Arkady") Darrell, though she does read more like a boy in a dress than an actual girl. One of the things Clarke and Asimov have in common is an inability to write females.

Heinlein, for me, is the greatest of the three, by such a huge margin that it's barely worth making the comparison. He is the only one of the three that actually has a literary style of his own, and his ability to plot and write dialogue is almost unmatched, not just in SF but in fiction generally. Of course it's because Heinlein is, in a sense, a literary writer in a way that the other two are not that he attracts stronger feelings, both positive and negative.

Heinlein's style is identifiably American, though tempered by British English. Like Hemingway he is an unashamedly masculine writer, and he controls his sentences far better than Asimov. Where Asimov is wordy and descriptive - see, for example, his paragraphs-long descriptions of the protagonists of "The Billiard Ball" - Heinlein rarely bothers with even a cursory physical description. Instead, we hear his characters speak, and see them in action, and their personalities are shown directly to the reader in the same way we form opinions of real people in the real world. Heinlein is also more romantic than either Asimov or Clarke. His romance, though, is not with women, but with a certain kind of mindset in either men or women. What Heinlein loves and idealises is the person who can both fit into an organised society and can act outside that society's rules when called on to do so. In this he is more like one person than any other: Kipling. It is surely no accident that Kipling's years of peak publication and wide circulation were those when Heinlein was growing up: Heinlein reads like Kipling in prose. Indeed, if I had to pick a single obvious precursor to Heinlein in SF history, it would be Kipling's "With the Night Mail". I would be astonished if Heinlein had not read and enjoyed Kipling: some of "Noisy" Rhysling's verse is so obviously in the same mode as Kipling's "McAndrew's Hymn" that the two cannot be unrelated.

Interestingly, Kipling inspires the same strong emotions as Heinlein, and for much the same reasons. Both are accused of chauvinism and racism, anti-feminism and imperialism, even though a careful reading of both shows precisely the opposite. Heinlein's ability to sneak non-white characters into a predominantly white genre in the 1950s shows a man who knew exactly what he was doing. I still remember reading "Starship Troopers" for the first time and realising Johnny Rico's ethnicity only at the very end of the book.

Heinlein's plotting skills are easy to admire - "All You Zombies" is merely the most famous of a long list that includes everything from "By His Bootstraps" to "Time Enough for Love" - but his dialogue is often overlooked. It takes huge technical skills to write multi-person conversations and keep everyone identifiable. Take a look at most writers: they can barely manage a three-way conversation. Then take a look at the opening family conversation in "The Rolling Stones" ("Space Family Stone"): seven people talking together, and you're never in doubt who's who.

I do agree that Heinlein's late-period writing is sometimes self-indulgent. His fear of death pervades his later work, but even then there are some gems: "Job" and "Friday" are wonderful, and although much of the "World as Myth" continuity is overblown there are still moments of immense cleverness in there. If I had to recommend any Heinlein I'd have to say "Read it All!", but if you want a good place to start, I'd begin with "The Door into Summer" and "The Puppet Masters", then try some of his "juveniles" (which, in reality, are perfectly suitable for all ages). If you want to read a perfect short story, read "Let There Be Light"; for a perfect novella, read "If This Goes On...", which has the added advantage of highlighting Heinlein's conception of America as a free republic in which religion has no place in the public square.

There is no writer for whom I have greater reverence that Heinlein. This isn't to say that he is flawless: he has his flaws as a writer, and had his flaws as a person, but as a clear-thinker, an individualist and a believer in the positive benefits of science he was, and is, without peer.
